chapter.name: Polynomials
chapter.blurb: Polynomials in one variable, their degree and standard names (linear, quadratic, cubic); the value and zeroes of a polynomial; the geometrical meaning of zeroes as x-intercepts of the graph of y = p(x), including the three cases for a quadratic and the degree-n-has-at-most-n-zeroes rule; and the relationship between the zeroes and coefficients of quadratic and cubic polynomials.

scope_in.item: Recognise whether an algebraic expression in one variable is a polynomial (only non-negative whole-number powers of the variable) and identify non-polynomial expressions such as 1/x + 1 or sqrt(x) + 2
Find the degree of a polynomial in one variable and classify it as linear (degree 1), quadratic (degree 2, ax^2 + bx + c) or cubic (degree 3, ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d), with a not 0 in each general form
Evaluate p(k), the value of a polynomial p(x) at x = k, by direct substitution
Define and test whether a given real number k is a zero of p(x), i.e. whether p(k) = 0
Find the zero of a linear polynomial ax + b algebraically as k = -b/a
Read the graph of a linear polynomial y = ax + b as a straight line meeting the x-axis at exactly one point, that point being the zero
Read the graph of a quadratic polynomial y = ax^2 + bx + c as a parabola (opening up if a > 0, down if a < 0) and identify its zeroes as the x-intercepts, using a table of values if needed

Distinguish the three cases for a quadratic graph -- two distinct x-intercepts, one repeated x-intercept (the graph touches the axis), or no x-intercept -- and state the corresponding zero count (2, 1 or 0)
State that a quadratic polynomial has at most 2 zeroes
Read the graph of a cubic polynomial to find its zeroes as x-intercepts, and state that a cubic polynomial has at most 3 zeroes
Apply the general rule that a polynomial of degree n has at most n zeroes, and count the zeroes of p(x) from a given graph of y = p(x) by counting x-axis intersections
Find the zeroes of a quadratic polynomial by splitting the middle term (factorisation)
State and use the relationship between the zeroes and coefficients of a quadratic ax^2 + bx + c: sum of zeroes = -b/a, product of zeroes = c/a
Verify the sum/product relationship for a quadratic given its zeroes, including cases needing the identity a^2 - b^2 = (a-b)(a+b)

Construct a quadratic polynomial ax^2 + bx + c when the sum and product of its zeroes are given, using alpha+beta = -b/a and alpha*beta = c/a, and recognise that k times that polynomial (k real, k not 0) also fits

State and use the relationship between the zeroes alpha, beta, gamma and coefficients of a cubic ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d: alpha+beta+gamma = -b/a, alpha*beta+beta*gamma+gamma*alpha = c/a, alpha*beta*gamma = -d/a
Verify the sum / pairwise-product-sum / product relationships for a cubic given its zeroes

concepts.name: Polynomials, degree and naming
concepts.description: Recognising an algebraic expression as a polynomial in one variable, finding its degree, and naming it linear, quadratic or cubic by that degree.
concepts.idea: A polynomial in one variable is built only from whole-number (non-negative) powers of that variable, added or subtracted with real-number coefficients; the highest power present is called its degree.
concepts.rule: Degree 1 is called linear (general form ax + b, a not 0); degree 2 is called quadratic (general form ax^2 + bx + c, a not 0); degree 3 is called cubic (general form ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d, a not 0).
concepts.example: 4x + 2 is linear (degree 1); 2y^2 - 3y + 4 is quadratic (degree 2); 5x^3 - 4x^2 + x - 2 is cubic (degree 3); but 1/x + 1 and sqrt(x) + 2 are not polynomials at all, since x appears with a negative or fractional power.

concepts.name: Value and zero of a polynomial; zero of a linear polynomial
concepts.description: Evaluating p(k) by substitution, defining a zero of p(x) as a real number k with p(k) = 0, and finding the zero of a linear polynomial algebraically.
concepts.idea: Putting a number in place of x in p(x) gives a single number, the value of p(x) at that point; when that value comes out to be exactly 0, the number substituted is called a zero of the polynomial.
concepts.rule: For p(x) = x^2 - 3x - 4, p(k) is found by replacing every x with k. A zero of p(x) is any real k with p(k) = 0. For a linear polynomial ax + b (a not 0), setting ak + b = 0 gives its one and only zero, k = -b/a.
concepts.example: For p(x) = x^2 - 3x - 4: p(2) = 4 - 6 - 4 = -6, so 2 is not a zero; p(-1) = 1 + 3 - 4 = 0 and p(4) = 16 - 12 - 4 = 0, so -1 and 4 are both zeroes. The zero of p(x) = 2x + 3 is -3/2.

concepts.name: Geometrical meaning of zeroes: lines and parabolas
concepts.description: Reading the zero(es) of a linear or quadratic polynomial off the graph of y = p(x) as its x-intercept(s), and the three possible cases for a quadratic's graph.
concepts.idea: The zeroes of p(x) are exactly the x-coordinates of the points where the graph of y = p(x) crosses or touches the x-axis, so counting crossing points tells you how many real zeroes the polynomial has.
concepts.rule: The graph of a linear polynomial y = ax + b (a not 0) is a straight line that meets the x-axis at exactly one point, so it has exactly one zero. The graph of a quadratic y = ax^2 + bx + c (a not 0) is a parabola (opening upward if a > 0, downward if a < 0) and it either (i) cuts the x-axis at two distinct points (2 distinct zeroes), (ii) touches the x-axis at one point / two coincident points (1 repeated zero), or (iii) does not meet the x-axis at all (no real zero). So a quadratic has at most 2 zeroes.
concepts.example: y = 2x + 3 crosses the x-axis only at (-3/2, 0). The graph of y = x^2 - 3x - 4 crosses the x-axis at x = -1 and x = 4, matching Table 2.1.

concepts.name: Geometrical meaning of zeroes: cubic graphs and the degree rule
concepts.description: Reading the zeroes of a cubic polynomial off its graph, and the general rule that a degree-n polynomial has at most n real zeroes.
concepts.idea: The x-intercept idea extends to any degree: a cubic's graph meets the x-axis in at most 3 points, and in general a degree-n polynomial's graph meets the x-axis in at most n points.
concepts.rule: A cubic polynomial has at most 3 zeroes. In general, a polynomial p(x) of degree n has at most n zeroes, and the graph of y = p(x) meets the x-axis in at most n points.
concepts.example: y = x^3 - 4x meets the x-axis at x = -2, 0, 2 (3 zeroes). y = x^3 meets it only at x = 0 (1 zero). y = x^3 - x^2 = x^2(x - 1) meets it at x = 0 and x = 1 (2 zeroes).

concepts.name: Relationship between zeroes and coefficients of a quadratic polynomial
concepts.description: Finding a quadratic's zeroes by splitting the middle term, and relating their sum and product to its coefficients.
concepts.idea: Once a quadratic is written as a product of two factors, k(x - alpha)(x - beta), comparing coefficients shows the sum and product of its zeroes are fixed, simple functions of a, b and c.
concepts.rule: For ax^2 + bx + c (a not 0) with zeroes alpha and beta: alpha + beta = -b/a (sum), and alpha * beta = c/a (product).
concepts.example: 2x^2 - 8x + 6 = 2(x-1)(x-3), zeroes 1 and 3: sum = 4 = -(-8)/2, product = 3 = 6/2. Given sum -3 and product 2, the polynomial x^2 + 3x + 2 fits, since -3 = -3/1 and 2 = 2/1.

questions.q: A student concludes that x^2 + 3x + 2 and 2x^2 + 6x + 4 must have different zeroes, since more terms means a 'different' polynomial. Evaluate this reasoning using the sum/product formulas.
questions.a: The reasoning is wrong. 2x^2 + 6x + 4 = 2(x^2 + 3x + 2), so both give sum = -3 and product = 2 (check: -6/2 = -3 and 4/2 = 2, same as -3/1 and 2/1), so they have exactly the same zeroes, -1 and -2. Multiplying a whole quadratic by a nonzero constant never changes its zeroes.
s: Recognises 2x^2 + 6x + 4 = 2(x^2 + 3x + 2)
Shows both give the same sum (-3) and product (2), so the same zeroes

concepts.name: Relationship between zeroes and coefficients of a cubic polynomial
concepts.description: Relating the sum, the sum of pairwise products, and the product of a cubic's three zeroes to its coefficients.
concepts.idea: The same coefficient-comparison idea used for quadratics extends to cubics, but a cubic's three zeroes give three separate relationships instead of two.
concepts.rule: For ax^3 + bx^2 + cx + d (a not 0) with zeroes alpha, beta, gamma: alpha + beta + gamma = -b/a, alpha*beta + beta*gamma + gamma*alpha = c/a, and alpha * beta * gamma = -d/a.
concepts.example: 2x^3 - 5x^2 - 14x + 8 has zeroes 4, -2 and 1/2: sum = 5/2 = -(-5)/2, pairwise sum = -7 = -14/2, product = -4 = -8/2.

questions.q: For the cubic 3x^3 - 5x^2 - 11x - 3, it is given that 3 and -1 are two of its three zeroes. (a) Using the product relationship alpha*beta*gamma = -d/a, find the third zero gamma. (b) State whether gamma is 1/3 or -1/3. (c) Verify using the sum relationship alpha + beta + gamma = -b/a.
questions.a: (a) -d/a = -(-3)/3 = 1, and alpha*beta = 3 * (-1) = -3, so gamma = 1/(-3) = -1/3. (b) gamma is -1/3, not 1/3. (c) Sum check: 3 + (-1) + (-1/3) = 5/3, and -b/a = -(-5)/3 = 5/3, which matches.
s: Correctly computes the product -d/a = 1 and sets up alpha*beta*gamma = 1
Correctly solves for gamma = -1/3 (not 1/3)
Verifies using the sum relationship, getting 5/3 both ways

questions.q: Create your own cubic polynomial (not already used in this chapter) with a = 1 and three zeroes of your choice. State the polynomial, and verify all three coefficient relationships (sum, pairwise-sum, product).
questions.a: For example, zeroes 2, -1 and -2. Sum = 2 + (-1) + (-2) = -1, so b = -(-1) = 1. Pairwise sum = (2)(-1) + (-1)(-2) + (-2)(2) = -2 + 2 - 4 = -4, so c = -4. Product = 2 * (-1) * (-2) = 4, so d = -(4) = -4. Polynomial: x^3 + x^2 - 4x - 4. Check: sum = -1 = -b/a = -1/1; pairwise sum = -4 = c/a = -4/1; product = 4 = -d/a = 4/1 -- all three match.
s: Chooses three zeroes and correctly computes their sum, pairwise sum and product
Correctly derives b, c, d and writes the cubic polynomial
Verifies all three coefficient relationships match
